_README: RECALL DENOMINATOR — threats a competent security reviewer WOULD expect the
model to find on the go-forward fixture, whether or not it actually did.
This file is the half a recorded snapshot can never contain. golden-threats.json
only holds what the model emitted, so on its own it can measure precision (of
what it said, how much was right?) but NEVER recall (of what was real, how much
did it find?). Without this file a prompt change that quietly stops finding a
whole class of threat is invisible.
Add entries by hand. Keep them at the abstraction level the product should
produce — the threat CLASS plus the affected asset or path, not an
implementation instance. 'If one mitigation closes both, it is one threat.'
componentId  must match a component in the fixture, or 'compound' for
threats that span components
category     STRIDE category
match        substrings, ANY of which marks this expectation satisfied.
Matched case-insensitively against the normalized threat name,
so wording drift does not produce a false miss.
rationale    why a reviewer expects this — the record of the judgement
Start with the obvious misses. A short, high-confidence list beats a long
speculative one: every entry here becomes a recall failure the team must
either fix or consciously accept.

_meta.authoredBy: security review — architecture-derived, not copied from golden
method: Derived from fixture-model.json (12 components, 15 connections) by reading
trust levels, data classifications, documented existingControls and per-edge
protocol/auth/encryption — NOT by reading golden-threats.json. An expectation
list written from the model's own output would score 100% and measure nothing.
Entries are at CLASS grain per the register's §5 rule: if one mitigation closes
both, it is one threat. Where a threat spans two components, it is filed against
the component that would implement the mitigation.
Deliberately short and high-confidence. Every entry here is a recall failure the
team must either fix or consciously accept, so speculative entries cost more

2026-08-17 — widened from 10 to 40. At 10 entries each expectation was worth 10 points of recall, so a single flickering finding swamped the metric and the ABSENT set reshuffled between samples. Entries are NOT written where a declared existingControl already covers the class: the prompt instructs the model to respect controls, so expecting the threat anyway would penalise obedience.

expected.rationale: Both edges into Redis carry encrypted=false while transporting session tokens and CONFIDENTIAL catalog data; the fixture even labels one 'Plaintext on the internal subnet — flagged risk'. Redis documents no existingControls at all.

All three service→Postgres edges authenticate with 'Basic' while carrying RESTRICTED data (PII, password hashes, invoices). Reusable static credentials on the system of record are a first-pass finding.

The end-user→portal edge is authentication=None and 'anonymous until login; session cookie afterwards', so session establishment is the trust hinge for a PUBLIC-facing component handling PII and cart contents.
Kong is the single JWT validation and routing choke point between the DMZ and INTERNAL zone. If its claim handling is wrong, every downstream authorization decision inherits the error.

The Auth Service description names password reset flows explicitly, and reset is the classic authentication bypass path (predictable or replayable reset tokens, reset-link leakage). It is the identity component, so a spoofing class here is expected.
'MFA secrets' is a declared dataType on this component. A second factor that can be skipped, re-enrolled, or brute-forced is a privilege escalation, and MFA appears nowhere in the current output.

Stripe 'returns charge results via webhook' per the payment-gateway description, but no inbound webhook edge is modelled and no signature verification is documented — a forged callback marks an unpaid order as paid. Filed against Billing because Billing implements the verification; one mitigation closes both sides, so it is one threat.

The component documents TDE and 'daily snapshots', but TDE protects the live volume — snapshot encryption, retention and access are not documented anywhere. A copy of the system of record is the highest-value disclosure path for a store holding PII and password hashes. (NB: the shipped example entry claimed 'no backup control documented', which the fixture contradicts — daily backups ARE listed. The gap is snapshot handling, not backup existence.)

SendGrid carries password-reset mail and order summaries — CONFIDENTIAL data leaving the trust boundary to an EXTERNAL_PARTNER. Reset links transiting a third party is a disclosure class distinct from the API-key handling already covered.

Redis is the session store, reachable with a shared API_KEY and no documented ACL. Anyone who can write a session key can mint an identity. Distinct from the transit-encryption class above: TLS does not fix it, authorization does.

Checkout submits cart contents from an UNTRUSTED actor over an auth=None edge. Server-authoritative pricing is the control; nothing in the fixture documents it, and WAF/CSP do not address business-logic tampering.
Declares session tokens and PII as dataTypes on a PUBLIC-access component. CSP headers reduce XSS delivery but do not govern where the app itself puts tokens.
Kong validates JWTs, but validity is not freshness: a captured token replays until expiry, and no token lifetime or binding is documented on the DMZ→internal hop.
JWT tokens are a declared dataType on a component whose job is to see every request. Token capture from access logs or verbose errors is the standard gateway disclosure class.
The single authentication decision point for the whole system. Without an audit trail of validation failures, credential attacks are unreconstructable after the fact.
Orchestrates order and billing operations carrying PII and auth claims, with no declared authorization control. Object-level authorization is the class an analyst expects on any resource-scoped API.
SOC2-scoped component handling PII with no error-handling control documented.
Accepts order data from the DMZ and forwards it to three internal services; it is the validation boundary for everything downstream.
Fans out to three gRPC services with no declared size or concurrency limit.
Declares password hashes, MFA secrets and refresh tokens as dataTypes. argon2 protects hashes at rest against cracking; it does not stop them reaching logs or error responses.

argon2 is a documented control and is deliberately expensive — which makes unthrottled login attempts a CPU-exhaustion vector. The control creates the threat; no rate limit is declared on this component.
Issues the credentials every other component trusts. Without an issuance audit trail, a forged-token incident cannot be scoped.
Writes order records to Postgres with no declared query-parameterization or validation control.
Exposes order lifecycle operations over gRPC; mTLS authenticates the caller but does not authorize the action.
Owns the order lifecycle — the record a customer or merchant would dispute.
PCI-DSS scoped, declares payment tokens as a dataType, and documents no control. Token leakage through logs or error paths is the first thing an assessor looks for.
Creates charges against a third-party gateway. If the amount is attacker-influenceable anywhere on the path, the loss is direct and monetary.
PCI-DSS Req 10 exists for this: financial operations need an attributable trail.
System of record for users, orders and invoices, written by three services none of which declare a parameterization control.
Holds password hashes and invoices. least-privilege roles limit who may write; they do not record who did.
Session store and catalog cache with no declared control and a shared API_KEY. Cache entries carry no integrity protection, so a write is indistinguishable from a legitimate one.
Holds sessions and catalog data with no declared eviction policy or memory bound — filling it logs every user out.
Carries order-placed and invoice-created events between services. Consumers act on messages they cannot verify.
Both publishers authenticate with Basic over a shared credential, so the broker cannot attribute a message to a specific service.
No declared rate limit or queue bound on the async backbone; a flood stalls order and billing processing together.
Order and billing events sit in the broker. Transport is encrypted; storage inside the broker is undocumented.
Reached with an API_KEY that authorizes real charges. Where that key lives and how it rotates is undocumented.
Charge creation is the highest-value operation in the system; who may invoke it is an application-side control that is not documented.
Sends order confirmations and password-reset mail built from application input. Header or content injection turns transactional mail into a phishing channel.
The only UNTRUSTED actor, entering over an auth=None edge. Account takeover against the public entry point is the highest-frequency real-world attack on a commerce platform.
